concerns: Assay interference by formulation excipients or device matrices could mimic loss of captured signal despite the planned compatibility panels; full buffer/compatibility validation is essential before interpreting stability outcomes (ev-misev2023-quality-framework).

Preservation of in vitro orthogonal signatures may not predict in vivo delivery or efficacy because route- and species‑specific clearance or nasal retention can prevent target access independently of product stability (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution).

The proposed readouts are largely qualitative; lack of quantitative thresholds or validated spike‑in behavior across matrices may reduce reproducibility and complicate comparability decisions—numeric or semi‑quantitative criteria would strengthen decision rules (ev-misev2023-quality-framework).

Protected‑cargo panels must be chosen to reflect putative functional cargo; current plan leaves selection to human decision — without linkage to mechanism there is risk the chosen cargo markers are not functionally relevant (ev-hermann-2023-neonatal-hi; ev-kodali-2017-status-epilepticus).

Even with in vitro discrimination of assay artifact vs true loss, labeling/detection artifacts and species differences in biodistribution mean the experiment alone cannot exclude in vivo delivery failure as an alternative explanation; planned short‑interval in vivo recovery studies are therefore a necessary next step (ev-driedonks-2022-macaque-biodistribution).
conclusion: Plausible and testable. The proposed orthogonal intact‑EV panel (capture co‑localization with particle peaks; detergent/protease protection; protected‑cargo fingerprint; particle:protein context) is consistent with ISEV/MISEV principles and with preclinical work showing processing/storage sensitivity in rodent EV efficacy studies. The experimental design includes appropriate within‑lot comparators, detergent/protease disruption controls, and capture‑compatibility/spike‑in controls to detect many assay artifacts, so it should discriminate assay interference from true loss of membrane/cargo in vitro. However, the design does not by itself establish that preserved in‑vitro signatures predict in‑vivo delivery or function (species/route clearance and labeling/detection issues remain plausible alternative explanations). Additional short‑interval in vivo recovery or potency linkage experiments using materials that pass/fail the proposed gates will be required to connect these stability attributes to downstream deliverability or biological effect.
evidence_gap: No direct evidence linking the proposed in vitro orthogonal intact‑EV signatures to in vivo delivery or functional potency across relevant species/routes. Non‑human primate data show intranasal retention and poor brain detection despite in vitro material, so an explicit short‑interval in vivo recovery/potency study using pass/fail materials (per the proposed attributes) is needed. Additional gaps: validation of capture‑compatibility across all candidate excipients and device/shear conditions; standardized exogenous intact‑EV spike‑in identity and dosing; and quantitative acceptance criteria (the proposal is qualitative/pass‑fail).
